title: Scaling Behavior of Discrete Diffusion Language Models
one_liner: Map how discrete diffusion language models scale under different corruption rules, so one can choose the right balance between data, compute, and model size.
lead: Language-model pretraining now lives under scaling laws: when data, compute, or model size change, different architectures respond differently. Discrete diffusion language models were proposed as an alternative to left-to-right generation, but earlier work suggested they need more data and more compute to catch up. This paper asks a more careful question: how much of that picture depends on the corruption rule used during training? The authors study a path between masked corruption and uniform corruption while controlling batch size and learning rate closely. They find that the scaling story changes with the corruption rule. Uniform corruption needs larger models but less data for compute-efficient training, which matters in data-constrained settings because the right corruption rule can change which resource is the true bottleneck.

problem.h2: Why scaling claims for discrete diffusion were incomplete
paras: When people compare language-model families, they usually ask how loss falls as compute, data, and model size increase. Earlier comparisons suggested that discrete diffusion models lag behind left-to-right models.

But those comparisons mixed together several design choices, especially the corruption rule used during training. In discrete diffusion, training repeatedly corrupts text and asks the model to recover the clean text. Masked corruption and uniform corruption hide information in different ways, so they may produce different scaling behavior. Without separating those cases, one can draw the wrong conclusion about whether the architecture itself is weak or whether one corruption rule is simply a poor fit for the data and compute regime.

callout.html: Study scaling by corruption rule instead of treating all discrete diffusion setups as one family, because the corruption rule changes the data and compute trade-off.

object.object: the scaling comparison used to judge discrete diffusion language models

hidden.name: how much useful signal survives each corruption level for a fixed compute budget
paras: The hidden quantity is not just final loss. It is how much recoverable information remains after corruption once one fixes the compute budget and the model size.

That quantity explains why two corruption rules can scale differently. If a corruption rule erases information in a way that larger models can still use well, then adding model size helps more because the extra capacity can recover more from the surviving clues. If it demands more observed text to learn the same recovery task, then data becomes the limiting resource. The paper's signal-to-noise view makes this trade-off easier to describe because the corruption rule directly controls how much useful signal survives.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark settings where the corruption rule leaves a usable learning signal for the available compute.

reads.html: The real issue is how much useful recovery signal remains after corruption once the training budget is fixed.
The study shows that scaling depends strongly on the corruption rule because each rule changes the signal-to-noise trade-off seen by the model during training.

mechanism.h2: Why the corruption rule changes scaling behavior
paras: A discrete diffusion model trains on corrupted text and learns to reverse that corruption. The corruption rule decides what the model sees and what it must reconstruct. That directly changes sample efficiency because some rules preserve more structure per example than others.

Masked corruption hides selected positions while leaving the rest untouched. Uniform corruption replaces content more broadly, which can demand a stronger model but may use each unit of compute with less waste when data are scarce because the model sees a broader reconstruction challenge per example.

The paper's careful tuning matters because poor batch-size or learning-rate choices can masquerade as architectural scaling limits. By controlling those settings, the authors show that much of the earlier pessimism about discrete diffusion came from mixing regimes. The reformulation in terms of signal-to-noise ratio also matters because it puts discrete diffusion closer to the language used in continuous diffusion theory, which makes the scaling picture easier to reason about and implement.

items.b: Scaling conclusions can be confounded by poor tuning.
items.html: If batch size or learning rate is mismatched across runs, one corruption rule can look worse simply because training was not equally optimized.

items.b: One corruption rule may dominate only in one regime.
items.html: A rule that is strong when data are scarce may lose its edge when data are abundant, because the resource bottleneck has changed.

items.b: Very large models may be required.
items.html: Uniform corruption can need a larger model before its efficiency benefit appears, so small-scale studies may underestimate it because the regime shift has not arrived yet.
With careful tuning and the right resource regime, discrete diffusion can scale competitively because the corruption rule can be matched to the available data and compute.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train small and medium discrete diffusion language models under masked and uniform corruption on the same text budget, while sweeping compute and data separately. Keep batch size and learning rate tuned for each family so the comparison reflects the corruption rule rather than poor optimization.

The demo should report loss against compute, loss against data, and the point where larger models start paying off. A convincing result shows the corruption rule changing the scaling frontier because the amount of recoverable signal per example changes with the rule.
demo.closing: The paper matters when the chosen corruption rule changes which resource is scarce, because that shifts the best training recipe for discrete diffusion models.
